lines: How checkout talks to the rest of us
a walkthrough for the on-call rotation
The four services on the path
A request comes in at the gateway, which owns auth and nothing else.
checkout holds the cart and the order.
checkout no longer writes Postgres directly — it calls ledger, which is now the only writer to orders.
payments talks to the card processor and is the only service with the key.
checkout calls ledger to write orders; ledger is the only writer to that table now.
payments keeps no state of its own; the processor is the record.
For the next two weeks, checkout dual-writes to Postgres and to ledger.
Postgres stays authoritative until the cutover; after that, ledger is the source of truth.
Both paths are live at once, so the two writes can disagree — that is what the 409 on the next slide means.
A 402 from payments is the processor, not us — check its status page first.
A 500 from checkout with no payments call in the trace is the order write.
A 409 from ledger means the dual-write disagreed; it is the migration, not the order.
Latency on POST /orders past two seconds is almost always the card processor, and the dashboard shows it per-service.
ledger writes the table now, and payments is still the only thing holding a key.
